extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric, aspiring public speakers, lawyers and orators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for composing and delivering public speeches in the classical (Roman) forum tradition, covering aims of oratory, the five constituent parts of speech, style, delivery, audience management, and common faults illustrated by historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three essential effects/duties of an Orator
rubrics_metrics.description: An Orator should be able to produce three principal effects on an audience (delight/admiration, secure assent/persuasion, and affect the passions/emotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text: one speaker's florid style excited admiration in the common audience; Crassus converted serious apprehension into mirth and good-humour (entertain); another speaker gained the assent of his hearers by arguing the testator's intention (persuasion). These three effects are presented as the core duties an Orator must be able to achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for unity and coherence (single plan, introduction, and peroration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defence (or cause) should be conducted on one uniform plan with a single natural introduction and conclusion; all parts should be regularly disposed and connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dividing a defence among multiple pleaders or assigning the peroration to a second advocate, since this breaks unity and weakens the connections between parts. Analogy: parts of a cause are like members of an animal body—they retain strength when regularly connected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention (finding appropriate arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The orator must have quick and fitting invention — the capacity to discover arguments most in point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antonius is praised for readily inventing pertinent arguments; Curio is criticized for being 'remarkably dull in the invention', showing how lack of invention undermines performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition/Arrangement (digesting and methodizing arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments must be well-digested and methodically arranged so the speech proceeds coherently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antonius digests and methodizes arguments to advantage; Curio's disposition is loose and unconnected, demonstrating that poor arrangement frustrates persuasive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elocution/Style (choice of words, purity, ornamentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language should be pure, neat, and appropriate to the speaker's style—either concise/neat or copious/dignified—without lapsing into dryness or empty parade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two classes of good orators: those distinguished by neatness and brevity, and those by copious dignity and elevation. The brief style must avoid dryness and poverty; the copious must avoid swelling, empty ornament. Examples: Cotta's neat, compact style; Sulpicius's florid, tragic style; Crassus's elegant language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation/Delivery (voice, gesture, action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery — strength and sweetness of voice, graceful and appropriate gesture, and control of bodily action — is essential to effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sulpicius praised for strong, sonorous, flowing voice and graceful gestures; Cotta prudently avoided forcible exertion because of weak lungs and adapted his language accordingly. Excessive or odd gestures (e.g., Titian jigg) invite ridicule and weaken a speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory (reliable retention and consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A trustworthy memory is required so the speaker does not forget parts of his planned speech or contradict himself, in both oral and written performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curio's frequent lapses of memory (adding or omitting heads of a speech, contradicting dates in written dialogues) caused ridicule and damaged his professional opportunities. Memory failures in capital trials are inexcusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and command the audience's passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A skilful orator must perceive how the audience is affected and know how to command their passions for the speech's ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A connoisseur can judge an orator's success from the judges' faces and demeanour (yawns, attention, signs of pity or abhorrence). The orator should aim to produce visible signs of emotional engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt style to audience and situation (learned vs. vulgar hearers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust rhetoric and style depending on whether the audience is the general public or a learned/cultured bench; what pleases the people may differ from the connoisseur's judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A speaker who delights the vulgar might be judged differently by an intelligent listener; the orator should be able to affect both kinds when necessary but be mindful of differing standards of taste and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wit, turns, and pleasantry to manage tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing wit and occasional pleasantry can defuse serious apprehension, entertain, and help secure assent when applied skillfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crassus used anecdotes and humor (the cock-boat tale) to take the edge off his opponent's strongest plea and convert the audience's mood to mirth and agreement; such enlivening should be used judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support arguments with precedents and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Augment persuasive force by adducing precedents, authorities, and a variety of views and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crassus supported his positions by a number of precedents and viewed questions from various angles; reliance on authoritative examples strengthens persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit method to pupil's natural bent and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should tailor instruction to a student's natural capacities—spur the quick, curb the timid—so that an orator's style matches innate character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to Socrates' treatment of pupils: observe natural genius and apply suitable discipline. Early domestic language and tutors strongly influence future oratorical ability (example: Curio's home education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid employing multiple pleaders on the same side
rubrics_metrics.description: Using several pleaders for one side leads to disadvantages: answering unheard points, inconsistent presentation, and loss of cohesive strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple speakers force subsequent pleaders to reply without hearing the original statements and break the unity and strength of a single sustained argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match exertion of voice and style to physical constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt vocal force and manner of speaking to the speaker's bodily strengths and weaknesses rather than forcing a style unsuited to constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cotta avoided forcible vocal exertion because of weak lungs and adapted his elocution accordingly, yet still achieved effective gentle emotion; imitation of others' physical delivery without regard to one's own body is unwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectations and oddities that may be parodied
rubrics_metrics.description: Steer clear of peculiar gestures, dress, or mannerisms that may amuse or be ridiculed and thereby damage credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Titian jigg (a dance invented from a speaker's awkward gesture) and other oddities that attract parody. Even if they gain attention, such affectations are dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use presence and dignity to compensate where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A dignified presence, graceful gesture, and authority of voice can compensate for deficiencies in invention or expression in some speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. Lentulus and others concealed poverty of invention by the mere dignity of their presence and correct gesture; action and bearing can be leveraged to sustain audience approval, though should not entirely replace substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning and knowledge as augmenting, not always necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Erudition in law, literature, and antiquities is valuable and can enhance an orator's authority, but great speaking skill can sometimes compensate for lack of formal learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some celebrated orators (e.g., Curio) had little learning yet achieved reputation through fluency and style; conversely, men of learning (e.g., Aelius, Varro) contributed by composing and supporting oratory without being performers themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and consistency in written works
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should ensure chronological and factual consistency when producing dialogues or speeches to avoid obvious blunders that discredit their arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curio's written dialogue mistakenly places events out of chronological order, an error that should have been caught on revision. Written performances require at least as much care as oral ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive vehemence or immoderate style
rubrics_metrics.description: Vehemence and immoderate eagerness may alarm listeners and reduce credibility; force must be controlled to match decorum and audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some orators poured forth rapid torrents and immoderate vehemence that made them seem like 'madmen' rather than persuasive speakers; balance passion with reasoned control.
